parole.testo: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish عادت (adet) (Turkish âdet), itself from Arabic عَادَة (ʕāda).
From Ottoman Turkish عقرب (ʼakreb, “scorpion”), from Arabic عَقْرَب (ʕaqrab).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish علیه السلام (ʼaleyhi s-selâm), from Arabic عَلَيْهِ ٱلسَّلَامُ (ʕalayhi s-salāmu).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish عالم (alem), from Arabic عَالَم (ʕālam).
Usually vocative, poetic. Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish امان (amân), from Arabic أَمَان (ʔamān, “tranquillity, peacefulness”).
From Ottoman Turkish آناصون (anason).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish عاشق (aşık), from Arabic عَاشِق (ʕāšiq).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish بایات (bayat), from Arabic بَائِت (bāʔit, “stale”).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish بقال (bakkal), from, Arabic بَقَّال (baqqāl).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish باروت (bârut), from Arabic بَارُود (bārūd)
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish بطانیه (battaniye, “blanket”), itself from Arabic بَطَّانِيَّة (baṭṭāniyya, “blanket”).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish بلا (bela, “calamity, misfortune, evil, trouble”). from Arabic بَلَاء (balāʔ).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish بكار (bekâr, “bachelor”), from Arabic بِكَر (bikar, “virgin”).

Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish بللور (billur), borrowed from Arabic بِلَّوْر (billawr), borrowed from Classical Persian بِلّور (billōr), from Middle Persian bylwl (/⁠*bēlūr⁠/), borrowed from Pali veḷuriya, from Proto-Dravidian *weḷ-ūr (name of a city) + Pali -iya.
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish بدلا (budala, “imbecile, fool”), from Arabic اَبْدَال pl (abdāl) of singular بديل (badīl).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish بخور (buhur, bahur, “incense”), from Arabic بَخُور (baḵūr, “incense”).
From Ottoman Turkish طاول (davul, “drum”), from Arabic طَبْل (ṭabl). Compare Greek νταούλι (ntaoúli).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish عرض (ırz), from Arabic عِرْض (ʕirḍ).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish عشق (eşk), from Arabic عِشْق (ʕišq).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish فائض (faʼiz), from Arabic فَائِض (fāʔiḍ).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish فال (fal, “fortune-telling”), from Arabic فَأْل (faʔl, “omen”).

parole.significato: A placeholder name for a person, used when a name is not known; a generic name; so-and-so
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish فلان (falan), from Arabic فُلَان (fulān).

Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish فنجان (fincan), borrowed from Arabic فِنْجَان (finjān), borrowed from Classical Persian پِنْگَان (pingān), possibly borrowed from Classical Syriac ܦܝܢܟܐ (pīnəḵā), from Aramaic פִּינְכָא (pīnəkā), borrowed from Ancient Greek πίναξ (pínax).
From Ottoman Turkish فستق (fıstık), from Arabic فُسْتُق (fustuq).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish فقرا, from Arabic فُقَرَاء (fuqarāʔ).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish غافل (gafil). from Arabic غَافِل (ḡāfil)
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish غنی (ganî), from Arabic غَنِيّ (ḡaniyy).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish غضب, from Arabic غَضَب (ḡaḍab).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish خبر (haber), from Arabic خَبَر (ḵabar).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish حیات (hayat), from Arabic حَيَاة (ḥayāh).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish خائن (ha'in, hayın, “traitor, mischievous”), from Arabic خَائِن (ḵāʔin, “traitor”).

Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish حق (hak, “the right, justice; a right; due, share; remuneration”), from Arabic حَقّ (ḥaqq, “truth”). The definition evolved from "right, claim, remuneration" > "claim to remuneration or justice" > "retribution, revenge".
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish خلا (halâ, helâ, “toilet, water closet”), from Arabic خَلَاء (ḵalāʔ).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish خلق (halk), from Arabic خَلْق (ḵalq). First attested in the 18th century by Frakulla.
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish حلقه (halka), from Arabic حَلْقَة (ḥalqa).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish حلوا, from Arabic حَلْوَى (ḥalwā) or حَلْوَاء (ḥalwāʔ).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish خاله (hala), from Arabic خَالَة (ḵāla, “maternal aunt”).
From Ottoman Turkish حبس (habs, “imprisonment, prison”), from Arabic حَبْس (ḥabs, “confinement”).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish خصم (hasm, hasım, “enemy”), from Arabic خَصْم (ḵaṣm).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish خطا (hata), from Arabic خَطَأ (ḵaṭaʔ).
From Ottoman Turkish خاطر (hatır), from Arabic خَاطِر (ḵāṭir).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish هوا (hava), from Arabic هَوَاء (hawāʔ).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish خندق (hendek), from Arabic خَنْدَق (ḵandaq).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish حیله (hile, “artifice, stratagem, ruse”), itself from Arabic حِيلَة (ḥīla, “trick, artifice, ruse”).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish حكم (hükm), from Arabic حُكْم (ḥukm).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish عبرت, from Arabic عِبْرَة (ʕibra, “example, lesson, warning”).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish ابریق (ibrik, ıbrık).

parole.significato: iftar, the evening meal that breaks each day's fast during Ramadan.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish افطار (iftar), from Arabic إفطار (ʔifṭār).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish علت (ʿillet), from Arabic عِلَّة (ʕilla).
From Ottoman Turkish امام (imam), from Arabic إِمَام (ʔimām).

parole.significato: a plant of the genus Coffea, coffee bean
parole.testo: From Ottoman Turkish قهوه (kahve, “coffee”), from Arabic قَهْوَة (qahwa, “coffee, a brew”). Another explanation claims it traces back to the name of the Kaffa region of Ethiopia, which is an Omotic word.

parole.significato: kaymakam, particularly (historical) as a kaza prefect in the Principality of Albania.
parole.testo: From Ottoman Turkish قایمقام (kaymakam), from Arabic مَقَام قَائِم (qāʔim maqām, “stand in”).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish قالای (kalay), from Arabic قَلَعِيّ (qalaʕiyy, “tin”).
From Ottoman Turkish قنطار (kantar), from Arabic قِنْطَار (qinṭār), from Ancient Greek κεντηνάριον (kentēnárion), from Latin centēnārium (“hundredweight”).
From Ottoman Turkish قرنفل (karanfil), from Arabic قَرَنْفُل (qaranful).

parole.significato: kaza, particularly (historical) as a former second-level administrative division of Albania
parole.testo: From Ottoman Turkish قضا (kaza, “division of a sanjak”), from Arabic قَضَاء (qaḍāʔ, “jurisdiction, court circuit”), from قَضَى (qaḍā, “to decide, to judge”).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish قمری (kumru), from Old Anatolian Turkish, from Arabic قُمْرِيّ (qumriyy, “laughing dove”).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish غربت (gurbet), from Arabic غَرَبَ (ḡaraba).

parole.significato: change (money given back when more than the exact price of an item is given)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish كسور (küsûr), from Arabic كُسُور (kusūr).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish قسمت (kısmet), from Arabic قِسْمَة (qisma). Compare Serbo-Croatian кѝсмет and Macedonian касмет (kasmet).
From Ottoman Turkish قسط (kıst, “id.”), from Arabic قِسْط (qisṭ, “equity; lot, portion, share”).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish لذت (lezzet, “taste; flavor; pleasure, enjoyment”). From Arabic لَذَّة (laḏḏa).
From Ottoman Turkish لقب (laḳab), from Arabic لَقَب (laqab).
From Ottoman Turkish لقمه (lukme, lokma), from Arabic لُقْمَة (luqma). Another variant is llomkë.
From Ottoman Turkish معدنوز (maydanoz), from Arabic مَعْدُونِس (maʕdūnis), from Byzantine Greek μακεδονήσιον (makedonḗsion, “parsley”).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish میمون (maymun), from Arabic مَيْمُون (maymūn).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish مصر (mısır), from Arabic مِصْر (miṣr).

parole.significato: mudir, particularly as a local official under Ottoman rule and during the Principality of Albania
parole.testo: From Ottoman Turkish مدیر (müdir, “local administrator, governor”), from Arabic مُدِير (mudīr, “directing one, governor, boss”), from أَدَارَ (ʾadāra, “to direct”).

parole.significato: refugee: most commonly used for Albanian communities which were expelled by the Serb Army mainly from the sanjak of Niš…
parole.testo: From Ottoman Turkish مهاجر (muhacir), from Arabic مُهَاجِر (muhājir).

parole.significato: mutasarrif, particularly (historical) as the governor of a sanjak under the Principality of Albania.
parole.testo: From Ottoman Turkish متصرف (mutasarrıf, “governor of a sanjak”), from Arabic مُتَصَرِّف (mutaṣarrif, “autonomous one, governor of a province”), from تَصَرَّفَ (taṣarrafa, “to act, to act independently”).
From Ottoman Turkish ناحیه (nâhiye), from Arabic نَاحِيَة (nāḥiya).
From Ottoman Turkish نفیس (“good, precious”), from Arabic نَفِيس (nafīs).

parole.significato: Infidel, atheist, pagan, non-believer, disbeliever, faithless, godless, heretic, miscreant ; a non-Muslim aside from ah…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish كافر (kafir), from Arabic كَافِر (kāfir, “denier, concealer”).

Unknown. Possibly borrowed from Ottoman Turkish قفا (compare Turkish kafa (“head”)), from Arabic قَفَاء (qafāʔ, “back of the neck”). However, the term is seen first in Buzuku's writings in 1555, and is present in the Arbëresh dialect as well, which usually does not have Turkish loans.
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish كاتب (ḱatib), from Arabic كَاتِب (kātib, “clerk”).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish كیف (keyf, literally “state, disposition”), from Arabic كَيْف (kayf, “state, disposition”).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish كرا (kira).
From Ottoman Turkish راف (raf), from Arabic رَفّ (raff), contaminated with rrafsh.
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish رشوت (rüşvet), from Arabic رِشْوَة (rišwa).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish ساعت (saʼat), itself derived from Arabic سَاعَة (sāʕa), ultimately from Aramaic שָׁעְתָא / ܫܳܥܬܳܐ (šāʿəṯā).

From Ottoman Turkish سراج (sarac, “saddler, saddlemaker”), itself from Arabic سَرَّاج (sarrāj, “saddler”), ultimately from Aramaic סַרָּגָא (sarrāgā) (in Classical Syriac ܣܰܪܳܓܳܐ), from סְרַג (srag, “to bind, to plait”) (in Classical Syriac ܣܪܰܓ).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish سبب (sebeb), from Arabic سَبَب (sabab).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish سلام علیکم (selam aleykum), from Arabic اَلسَّلَام عَلَيْكُم (as-salām ʕalaykum, “peace be upon you”).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish سلامت (selamet), from Arabic سَلَامَة (salāma).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish سودا (sevda), from Arabic سَوْدَاء (sawdāʔ).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish شیطان (şeytân), from Arabic شَيْطَان (šayṭān).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish شكر (şükr, vulg. şükür, “thankfulness, gratitude”), itself derived from Arabic شُكْر (šukr).
From Ottoman Turkish [script needed] (suret), from Arabic صُورَة (ṣūra).

parole.significato: circumcision (especially for observance of Islamic religious customs)
parole.testo: From Ottoman Turkish سنت (sünnet), from Arabic سُنَّة (sunna).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish ترتیب (tertip), from Arabic تَرْتِيب (tartīb).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish تسبیح (tesbih), from Arabic تَسْبِيح (tasbīḥ).
From Ottoman Turkish وعده (vaʼde), from Arabic وَعْدَة (waʕda).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish والله (vallâhi), from Arabic وَاللهِ (wallāhi, “by God”).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish وطن.
From Ottoman Turkish وسوسه (vesvese, fesfese), from Arabic وَسْوَسَة (waswasa, “suggestion of the devil, temptation”).

parole.significato: vilayet, particularly (historical) as a former first-level division of the Ottoman Empire
parole.testo: From Ottoman Turkish ولایت (vilayet, “province”), from Arabic وِلَايَة (wilāya, “province, administration”).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish جامع (cami), from Arabic جَامِع (jāmiʕ).
From Ottoman Turkish جهنم (cehennem), from Arabic جَهَنَّم (jahannam).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish جیب (ceb, cep), from Arabic جَيْب (jayb, “pocket”).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish جن (cin), from Arabic جِنّ (jinn).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish جمعه, from Arabic الْجُمْعَة (al-jumʕa).

parole.significato: zaptieh (law enforcer within the Ottoman Empire, similar to modern police forces)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish ضبطیه (zabtiye, “policeman”), from Arabic ضَبْطِيَّة (ḍabṭiyya, “policeman”), from ضَبْط (ḍabṭ).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish زار (zar, “die”), from Arabic زَهْر (zahr, “cube, die”).
Likely borrowed from Ottoman Turkish ظَرْف, ultimately from Arabic ظَرْف (ẓarf, “container”).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish زفت (zift, “pitch, tar”), from Arabic زِفْت (zift, “pitch, tar”).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish ضیافت (zıyâfet, ziyâfet), from Arabic ضِيَافَة (ḍiyāfa), verbal noun of ضَافَ (ḍāfa).
